Learning Objectives
Identify treatment options for acute and chronic tibialis anterior tendon ruptures.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
The most common types of tendon pathology include lacerations and closed ruptures.
Closed ruptures are the result of a strong eccentric contraction in younger individuals or
attritional ruptures in older patients with diabetes mellitus, with inflammatory arthritis, or who
have had previous local steroid injections.

Laceration
Rupture

Anatomy and Biomechanics
Vascular Anatomy
Proximally: anterior tibial artery
Distally: branches of medial tarsal artery
Posteriorly, the tendon has a complete vascular network from the musculocutaneous junction
to the insertion; however, anteriorly, an avascular zone 4.5 to 6.7 cm in length correlates with
the most common sites of spontaneous rupture.
Nerves
The tibialis anterior muscle is innervated by the deep peroneal nerve (L4) and originates
primarily from the anterolateral tibia.
Tendons
The tibialis anterior tendon passes beneath the superior and inferior extensor retinaculum
and inserts on the medial aspect of the base of the first metatarsal and the medial cuneiform.
It acts as the primary dorsiflexor of the ankle but also inverts the hindfoot.
The muscle dorsiflexes the foot in preparation for heel strike during the late swing phase of
gait; it eccentrically contracts after heel strike to slow progression until the foot is flat.
Musculature
Originates along the anterolateral tibia and inserts onto the medial aspect of the first
metatarsal and the medial cuneiform
Functions concentrically during the swing phase of gait to dorsiflex the ankle and allow
clearance of the foot
At heel strike, the tendon works in an eccentric fashion to control the progression to the
foot’s flat position.
This progressive relaxation of the muscle allows the hindfoot to assume a more valgus
posture, unlocking the Chopart joint and creating a more mobile foot to accommodate
uneven surfaces.
As the foot progresses towards toe-off, concentric contraction progresses

The anterior tibial tendon assists with inversion of the foot, creating a rigid lever that propels
the body forward.
Etiology
Rare in a normal tendon unless by sudden force or laceration.
Spontaneous ruptures are the result of degenerative process or local corticosteroid injections.
The anterior tibial tendon, without underlying pathology, rarely ruptures unless a laceration
(penetrating injury) is present or sudden force occurs.
Spontaneous rupture occurs secondary to a degenerative process, usually in males aged 50 to
70 years.
The usual site of a rupture is 0.5 to 3 cm proximal to its insertion, at the location at which the
tendon passes beneath the inferior extensor retinaculum.
Risk Factors
The causes of spontaneous rupture are degenerative in nature.
Inflammatory arthritis
Autoimmune disorders
Diabetes mellitus
Infection
Ischemia
Hyperparathyroidism
Gout
Obesity
Oral or previous local steroid therapy
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patients with chronic tibialis anterior tendon injuries report difficulty in clearing the foot during
gait (footdrop).
In the acute setting, the patient reports a pop followed by swelling in the anterior ankle. This
may be mistaken for an ankle sprain, leading to a delay in diagnosis. A prodrome of pain may
occur followed by a relief of that pain as the tendon ruptures.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/4/26, 9:55 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002005
3/17

Patient History
Pain may be minimal after the initial incident.
Therefore, pain does not often lead a patient to see a provider.
Instead, a patient is likely to report a foot slap or unsteady gait, limping, or increased fatigue
with walking.
The rupture may have a prodrome of swelling/pain or may follow a twisting or hyperplantar
flexion moment to the ankle.
After the injury, the initial pain subsides fairly rapidly, and compensation by the other extensor
muscles crossing the anterior ankle may mask the deficient anterior tibial tendon.
Therefore, the diagnosis of rupture often is missed or delayed.
Only after patients resume attempted normal gait do they realize they have difficulty with
walking due to footdrop.
They fatigue walking longer distances or for longer time intervals, and the compensatory
extensor tendons fatigue.
Physical Examination
Swelling anteriorly in the acute setting, but this may be minimal in the chronic setting (Figure
1)
A steppage gait pattern may be observed.
Weakness in dorsiflexion and lack of a palpable anterior tibial tendon during resisted
dorsiflexion
Increased extension at the metatarsophalangeal joints of the toes, especially when walking as
the extensor tendons attempt to compensate for loss of dorsiflexion power
Inability to heel walk because the functioning extensor tendons do not have sufficient power
to sustain active dorsiflexion

Figure 1 Clinical photographs of the feet and ankles of two separate patients. A, Photograph
shows a chronic, right anterior tibialis tendon rupture. Note the loss of normal tendon definition
(longer yellow arrow) about the anteromedial ankle compared with the contralateral side (shorter
yellow arrow). In addition, note the extensor hallucis longus and extensor digitorum longus
tendon recruitment (red arrows), evidenced by the relative hyperextension observed at the toe
metatarsophalangeal joints. B, Photograph shows a chronic, left anterior tibialis tendon rupture.
Note the loss of normal anterior tibialis tendon contour over the ankle (yellow arrows) and the
relative hypertrophy of the extensor hallucis longus tendon (red arrow) because of secondary
recruitment for ankle dorsiflexion. (Reproduced from Chen J, Kadakia R, Akoh CC, Schweitzer KM
Jr: Management of anterior tibialis tendon ruptures. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2021;29[16]:691-701.)
Neurovascular Examination
Analyze the patient’s gait for slapping of the foot caused by insufficient dorsiflexion and
supination resulting in an inability to clear the floor during swing phase.
Substantial to minimal foot drop also may be present secondary to uncontrolled plantar
flexion.
Provocative testing shows decreased range of motion and dorsiflexion strength of the foot (L4)
as compared to spared extensor hallucis longus strength (L5).
Increased eversion may be present during dorsiflexion secondary to the unopposed pull of the
peroneals.
If a herniated disk is suspected, eversion (L4) would also be weak.
Those with spine pathology also may have dermatomal sensory abnormalities.
Imaging Studies

Radiography
Radiographs typically are not necessary but help rule out other pathology.
In acute situations, anterior swelling may be observed on lateral radiographs.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI can be performed to identify a tendon rupture or incomplete tear, particularly in patients
without any antecedent trauma (Figure 2).
This imaging modality is very useful for determining the site of rupture and the quality of the
residual tendon.
Helpful in planning surgical management (repair vs reconstruction)
Figure 2 Images of an ankle with an anterior tibialis tendon rupture. Sagittal (A) and axial (B)
proton density MRIs show an anterior tibialis tendon attritional rupture with a retracted tendon
stump because of impinging anteromedial ankle osteophytes (red arrows). An empty tendon
sheath sign (yellow arrow) is observed near the anteromedial ankle. C, Intraoperative photograph
shows the chronic anterior tibialis tendon rupture and the underlying ankle osteophytes after
ankle arthrotomy. These osteophytes will be resected to decompress the region for planned
anterior tibialis allograft tendon reconstruction. (Reproduced from Chen J, Kadakia R, Akoh CC,
Schweitzer KM Jr: Management of anterior tibialis tendon ruptures. J Am Acad Orthop Surg
2021;29[16]:691-701.)
On MRI, disorder and tendon rupture are indicated by gapping and focal high signal intensity
compared with surrounding tissue
The gap length should be noted.

Sagittal, fat-suppressed, T2-weighted fast spin-echo MRI visualizes the retracted, torn tibialis
anterior, which may correspond with the palpable mass on physical examination.
The torn end of the tendon may display a thickened bulbous morphology, with increased
intrasubstance signal. Sagittal T1-weighted MRI also may show a torn tibialis anterior (Figure
3).
At the level of the ankle, the tibialis anterior that is normally observed in cross-section as a
black oval structure anterior to the joint has an empty tendon sheath, distended with
hyperintense material on T2-weighted MRI, but the tendon is not visible.
Figure 3 Sagittal (A) and axial (B) T1-weighted MRIs of an ankle show a chronic anterior tibialis
tendon rupture. Note the bulbous-shaped, degenerative proximal tendon stump (arrows)
retracted to just proximal to the level of the anterior ankle joint at the superior extensor
retinaculum, resulting in the classic pseudotumor appearance for this injury noted on physical
examination. (Reproduced from Chen J, Kadakia R, Akoh CC, Schweitzer KM Jr: Management of
anterior tibialis tendon ruptures. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2021;29[16]:691-701.)
Ultrasonography
Ultrasonography is a useful tool to evaluate the dynamic function of the anterior tibial tendon
and its sheath.

With more subtle or linear fissuring, ultrasonography may provide additional value in detecting
tendon quality.
Particularly useful in observing how the tendon glides through the sheath
Pathology
In a histologic review of 891 spontaneously ruptured tendons, Kannus and Józsa1 reported
that all specimens were structurally abnormal, with 97% showing degenerative changes.
The idea that complete rupture is a culmination of a degenerative process and, therefore, is
preceded by tendinosis, with or without tenosynovitis, intrasubstance tears, and partial tears,
seems logical.
Differential Diagnosis
Other causes of drop foot
Acute or chronic L4-L5 radiculopathy
Common peroneal palsy/neuropathy
Central nervous system (brain, spinal cord, nerve roots)
Peripheral nervous system (sciatic nerve, peroneal nerve)
Traumatic (knee dislocation, laceration, blunt trauma)
Compressive (compressive mass, deformity correction)
Systemic (diabetic polyneuropathy, mononeuropathy)
Iatrogenic (laceration, casting, positioning, surgical injury)
Mechanical (muscle débridement, tumor excision, etc.)
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Indications
In low-demand or elderly patients, bracing management of acute or chronic rupture with the
use of an ankle-foot orthosis is acceptable. (Resource 1)

Indications

8/17

However, patients must understand that the length deficit of the anterior tibial tendon
will not improve with time, and they are unlikely to recover substantial dorsiflexion
function even with aggressive physical therapy. No relevant randomized prospective
studies have been published. Available research is primarily composed of case reports
and small studies, most of which recommend early direct repair to restore function.2,3
Surgical Management
Indications
No general consensus exists with regard to whether anterior tibial tendon ruptures should be
managed surgically or nonsurgically.
Outcome studies are limited by the number of case reports and case series cited in the
literature.3,4
Management goals
Relieve pain
Improve function with consideration of patient age, chronicity of the injury, baseline
functional capacity, and medical comorbidities
In general, young, active, healthy, and high-functioning patients benefit from surgical
treatment.
Patients in whom an ankle-foot orthosis fails or in whom an Achilles tendon contracture
develops may benefit from surgical treatment.
Elderly, ill, or low-demand patients can be treated appropriately via immobilization in an
ankle-foot orthosis.
The chronicity of the injury also is an important factor because ruptures older than 4 weeks
may result in greater tendon retraction, limiting the ability for direct repair.
In patients with an acute laceration or rupture, the tendon can retract beneath the extensor
retinaculum and become adherent to nearby structures.
Urgent surgical management of acute injuries reduces the likelihood of retraction and
contracture that may hinder the ability to perform primary repair.
In patients with a chronic rupture, a defect may need to be bridged via an adjacent tendon
transfer or free graft.
In patients with a chronic injury, recognition of secondary deformities, such as
gastrocnemius or Achilles tendon contractures, that may prevent maximum dorsiflexion

9/17

during repair or reconstruction is important.
Complete Ruptures
In the acute setting, end-to-end repair is performed if the tendon is relatively normal.
The injury may be a rupture near the tendon insertion and may require suture anchors or
bone tunnels for appropriate fixation.
Débridement, V-Y lengthening (if necessary for tendon apposition), and repair are the best
options if a healthy tendon is available for repair.
To restore active dorsiflexion to the ankle in patients who have an insufficient tibialis anterior
tendon with a chronic rupture or attritional disease, free allograft interposition can be
performed if good muscle excursion remains or extensor hallucis longus tenodesis can be
performed if muscle excursion is limited.
Partial ruptures or lacerations can be managed via casting alone.
Progression to complete rupture can occur after casting; therefore, casting in patients with
atrophy may result in secondary rupture during attempts to regain strength with a
compromised (pathologic) tendon.
Prophylactic repair of partial ruptures is dependent on the typical activity level of the
patient.
Chronic Ruptures
Indications for allograft reconstruction
Chronic rupture with retraction
A defect greater than 3 to 4 cm
Prevent the morbidity associated with tendon transfer or autograft reconstruction

Chronic Ruptures
Studies have described several techniques for allograft reconstruction using
semitendinosus, gracilis, peroneus longus, anterior tibial tendon, and Achilles tendon
allografts.5,6 Allografts are available with bone block attachment or free tendon ends,
which can be anchored with the use of drill holes or via primary suture repair; various
hardware options are available for autograft fixation

Techniques/Procedures
Preoperative Planning
MRI or ultrasonography to evaluate the location of tendon retraction
Patient Positioning
Supine
Surgical Approaches
A curvilinear incision is made over the tibialis anterior tendon, with care taken to protect the
cutaneous nerves (Video 1).
The tibialis anterior tendon sheath is opened, and the tendon is exposed.
The tendon is examined for evidence of tendinosis and a split tear.
The tendon ends are excised, especially if they are tendinopathic.
Options for repair include Z-lengthening with side-to-side anastomosis or direct end-to-end
repair via a Bunnell, Krackow, or modified Kessler suture technique.
Depending on the level of rupture, nonanatomic repair may be performed to reconstruct
the anterior tibial tendon.
In patients with a distal rupture or avulsion fracture, the tendon can be reconstructed with
a suture anchor in the navicular, the first cuneiform, or a horizontal drill hole to pass the
tendon and suture it to itself.
If an allograft is used, tibialis anterior tendon allograft typically is used
The distal end is secured into the cuneiform with the use of a tenodesis screw or suture
anchor.
The ankle is dorsiflexed beyond neutral before setting tension.
The allograft tendon is secured via Pulvertaft weave into the native tibialis anterior.
During closure, the tendon sheath is repaired; however, differences exist in techniques
regarding the role of the extensor retinaculum after repair.

Management of anterior tibialis tendon ruptures. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2021;29(16):691-701.
Postoperative Management
Non–weight bearing for 4 to 6 weeks postoperatively, followed by physical therapy and
walking in a controlled ankle motion boot for 6 weeks
Complications
Possible complications of surgical management
Decreased dorsiflexion strength
May manage with the use of an ankle-foot orthosis
Re-rupture of repair
This may be because of the quality of the repair, tightness of the Achilles tendon and/or
the repair itself, poor quality tissue at repair site, or infection.
After determining the etiology of the failure, may need to use autologous or allograft
tissue
Formation of adhesions between the tendon and the extensor retinaculum
May need to débride and protect with the use of a tendon-protecting membrane
Complications inherent to surgical management (pullout of tendon, disruption of the
primary repair site (Figure 4).

Outcomes
No randomized prospective studies are available to guide the management of anterior tibial
tendon ruptures; only case reports and relatively small retrospective case studies have been
published.2,3
